podcast.body: A significant funk and soul excursion that became a number one hit on the US Hot 100, showcasing Bowie's appeal in America. However, its chart performance differed significantly in the UK, where it only reached number 17. "Fame was a number one hit on our Hot 100, only a number 17 hit in the UK."

podcast.body: Co-written by David Bowie and John Lennon, this song originated from a conversation they had about the difficulties of being famous, with the lyrics co-written in about 20 minutes. It features Bowie's lead vocals and Lennon's background vocals (emphasizing "fame" in the verses). Although Bowie reportedly didn't like the song much and it was tacked onto the "Young Americans" album at the last minute, it was released as a single and became his first ever number one hit in America. "And it became Bowie's first ever number one in America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Co-written in the studio by Bowie, John Lennon, and Carlos Alomar, this biting, spiteful song was a kiss-off to Bowie's former manager, Tony DeFries. Released as the second single from 'Young Americans' in summer 1975, it became David Bowie's first single to reach number one in America, also crossing over to number 23 on Billboard's Soul Singles Chart and being perceived as de facto disco on Top 40 radio. "Released as the second single from Young Americans in the summer of 75, Fame did something no David Boey single had ever done. It went all the way in America."
